The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler.

Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero.

Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services.

The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.

British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. British families are left to pay for it with lower wages, longer waits for a GP appointment and homes they cannot afford. Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society.

Pritzker announced on Tuesday that his state will not opt into the program, which was signed into law by President Donald Trump last year as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. "At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education – especially as the Trump Administration's policies decimate education," Pritzker said in a statement. "We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics."

The program allows people to receive federal tax credits for donations up to $1,700 to authorized scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs), which distribute the donated scholarship funds to eligible families to be used on private or public educational…

The criminal case centered on Trump's reimbursement of his then-attorney Michael Cohen, who paid adult film actress Stormy Daniels $130,000 shortly before the 2016 election to keep her from publicizing an alleged sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier. 

Trump, who denies the encounter, was found guilty in May 2024 of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records.

items.title: Why deep pockets weren’t enough to save the GOP in 2026: 'Money is not magic'
items.summary:
Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration.

Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov.

Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters.

It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity.

items.title: Troubling side effects of Walz’s signature legislation triggering local outrage as he heads for the exit
items.summary:
Minnesota’s new paid leave law, championed and signed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, is already causing major headaches as public employees take advantage of the program at levels that are straining government services.

Eleven months after the law took effect — allowing Minnesota workers up to 12 weeks a year off with partial pay to care for a newborn or a sick family member, and up to 12 weeks to recover from their own serious illness — almost one in four Minneapolis city employees has used the benefit, the Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

The outlet reported that the absences are putting a "squeeze" on some departments, including the agency that takes emergency calls in the city.

On Tuesday, a clip posted by Alpha News from an October budget presentation to the Minneapolis City Council went viral on social media. In the video, Emergency Communications Center Assistant Director Leticia Cardenas tells the council that 41% of her 911 staff were out on Minnesota’s new Paid Family and Medical Leave program.

items.title: Federal grand jury hears evidence in Ilhan Omar investigation, as court records use 3 versions of her name
items.summary:
A federal grand jury in Minnesota is hearing evidence in the investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., sources told Fox News.

Federal prosecutors described the case in newly unsealed court records as a "pre-indictment investigation." It remains unclear what evidence the panel has heard or whether it will return charges.

There are at least two active investigations underway, according to sources: One into allegations of immigration fraud and another into Omar's finances.

ILHAN OMAR APPEARS CLUELESS ON BASIS FOR FEDERAL PROBES: ‘YOU PROBABLY HAVE MORE DETAILS ON THAT’

Omar has repeatedly denied wrongdoing to Fox News Digital in connection with the investigations, but the investigations remain ongoing, and no official charges have been filed to date. The immigration investigation reportedly originated under then-President Barack Obama, while former President Joe Biden's administration opened the investigation into her finances.

In a detail sources say is relevant to the immigration probe, court records use three versions of Omar’s name. Investigators are examining whether she used a false name or birthdate to obtain U.S. citizenship.

items.title: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one

These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape.

To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett, was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist
items.t: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes

items.title: Still racist, misogynistic and homophobic. I’m putting Britain’s biggest police force on notice – we won’t tolerate this | Sadiq Khan
items.summary:
Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I

In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree.

Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most.

Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP.

items.title: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'
items.summary:
Kroger, the largest traditional grocery chain in the nation, is facing strong blowback on social media over its plan to slash 3,000 jobs in the United States while advertising new positions overseas in India.

The controversy comes as the Cincinnati-based grocer begins executing a three-year plan it has previously announced to cut $5 billion in costs as part of a restructuring that will eliminate roughly 37% of its U.S. corporate workforce by 2029.

While Kroger maintains the reductions are aimed at lowering shelf prices through technology and leaner operations, simultaneous recruiting for a new hub in Bangalore has fueled online accusations that the company is offshoring American jobs while asking shoppers to bear high food prices.

"‘They’re doing the jobs Americans don’t want to do,’" Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first term, posted on X. "No. They are taking jobs from Americans because it’s cheaper for corporations to hire foreigners."
items.t: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'

Congress is nearing the deadline to avert a government shutdown, and Senate Republicans are taking a leap of faith as the clock ticks: trusting Senate Democrats to dodge a holiday disaster.

When the upper chamber returns on Nov. 30, there will be just shy of two weeks for both sides to reach an agreement to thwart another partisan closure. At the center of the issue is the Iran war: Democrats intend to use the government’s purse strings to bring the eight-month conflict to an end.

Republicans, meanwhile, want to put together an emergency supplemental funding package with hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to the military, munitions and war effort. They have, for now, pressed pause on ramming those tax dollars through the party-line budget reconciliation process, and instead are opening the door to work with Democrats.

DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN

There’s history here: Senate Democrats have twice now ushered in a government shutdown. And though Republicans agreed behind closed doors to move forward with their counterparts, they know it’s a leap in the dark.

"Each side is a gamble," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, obviously, if it's party-line, when you look at the House side, you know, we got…

items.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
items.summary:
Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back

Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television?

Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis.

Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian

items.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
items.summary:
Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance

Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it. Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal?

Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK.

items.t: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial

The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style

As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations.

In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. items.title: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan
items.summary:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

items.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
items.summary:
Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life

Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing.

Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.”

items.title: The next fight for democracy is in the states | Stacey Abrams
items.summary:
Defend those being targeted, even when the threat has not reached your door

Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with bold ideas for America’s political future. Today’s edition was written by Stacey Abrams, a voting rights activist, author, and former Georgia house minority leader.

On 3 November, from Arizona to Georgia to Pennsylvania to Wisconsin, where a 16-year Republican majority fell, voters flipped at least 12 legislative chambers, the strongest statehouse showing for pro-democracy candidates since 2008. This did not happen by chance.

Our democracy will be measured by what we protect, what we build and whom we refuse to leave behind.

items.title: Talk of scrapping Natural England smacks of a government not joining the dots
items.summary:
Environmentalists say abolishing independent body will make it easier for landowners and developers ‘to trash nature’

Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.

Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.
